steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our survey paper on AI-generated text forensics. It should motivate the problem with LLM misuse, lay out the three pillars our survey is organized around (detection, attribution, characterization), and position the survey against existing surveys.

steps.text:

- AI-generated text forensics and its three pillars
- Why this survey; first systematic review

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4, Gemini, and also open-source ones such as Falcon and Llama 1&2 have greatly improved what is possible in natural language generation. Because of these advancements it is now possible to produce text that is grammatically correct and also very persuasive, and it is close to human-written content. These models are useful in many domains like journalism, academia, and social media, where they are powerful tools that make content creation faster. However, these models also bring big challenges, especially when it comes to information integrity. People are more and more concerned that LLMs could be misused to generate and spread misinformation, propaganda, and disinformation, which undermines public trust and the foundations of democracy.

To address these concerns we need a focused study of 'AI-generated text forensics.' This is an emerging field that is about developing methods for analyzing, understanding, and mitigating the misuse of AI-generated text. In this survey we introduce the pillars of AI-generated text forensics, shown in Figure 1: (i) detection, (ii) attribution, and (iii) characterization. Each of these has its own purpose in fighting the misuse of AI-generated content. Detection is about telling apart human and AI-generated texts, and it is a fundamental step for protecting information integrity. Attribution goes further and traces the AI-generated content back to the model it came from, which helps transparency and accountability. Characterization tries to understand what the intent behind the AI-generated text is, which is important for preempting harmful content.

- Why this survey
  - first systematic review of AI-generated text forensic systems; taxonomy in Figure 2
  - evolving sophistication of AI text + misuse -> multi-faceted approach needed
  - organize current work, identify gaps, future directions
  - more robust, transparent, accountable digital information ecosystems
- Related surveys
  - existing surveys: detection, attribution, in isolated contexts
  - ours: broad themes, fundamental pillars, interconnections, challenges as AI text becomes pervasive

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4, Gemini, and also open-source ones such as Falcon and Llama 1&2 have greatly improved what is possible in natural language generation. Because of these advancements it is now possible to produce text that is grammatically correct and also very persuasive, and it is close to human-written content. These models are useful in many domains like journalism, academia, and social media, where they are powerful tools that make content creation faster. However, these models also bring big challenges, especially when it comes to information integrity. People are more and more concerned that LLMs could be misused to generate and spread misinformation, propaganda, and disinformation, which undermines public trust and the foundations of democracy.

To address these concerns we need a focused study of 'AI-generated text forensics.' This is an emerging field that is about developing methods for analyzing, understanding, and mitigating the misuse of AI-generated text. In this survey we introduce the pillars of AI-generated text forensics, shown in Figure 1: (i) detection, (ii) attribution, and (iii) characterization. Each of these has its own purpose in fighting the misuse of AI-generated content. Detection is about telling apart human and AI-generated texts, and it is a fundamental step for protecting information integrity. Attribution goes further and traces the AI-generated content back to the model it came from, which helps transparency and accountability. Characterization tries to understand what the intent behind the AI-generated text is, which is important for preempting harmful content.

As far as we know, this is the first systematic review on AI-generated text forensic systems, and it has a detailed taxonomy which is shown in Figure 2. We need this work because AI-generated text is getting more sophisticated and can be misused, so a multi-faceted approach is required for analysis and mitigation. So this survey aims to organize the current work and to identify the gaps and the future directions in this field, which is developing fast. Our work helps to advance research in AI-generated text forensics and contributes to building digital information ecosystems that are more robust, transparent, and accountable.

Related Surveys: There are many surveys that discuss aspects of detection and attribution, but in isolated contexts. Our survey is different, because its objective is to outline the broad themes in the AI-generated forensics field by identifying its fundamental pillars, exploring how they are connected, and discussing challenges while envisioning a future where AI-generated text is pervasive.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 [1], Gemini [2], and open-source variants such as Falcon [3] and Llama 1&2 [4] has significantly enhanced natural language generation capabilities. These advancements make it possible to produce text that is not only grammatically correct but also highly persuasive, closely resembling human-written content. These models are used in various domains such as journalism, academia, and social media, where they serve as powerful tools for streamlining content creation. However, these models also introduce substantial challenges, particularly for information integrity. There is growing concern over the potential misuse of LLMs to generate and spread misinformation, propaganda, and disinformation, thus undermining public trust and the foundations of democracy [5,6].

Addressing these concerns requires a focused study of 'AI-generated text forensics,' an emerging field dedicated to developing methods for analyzing, understanding, and mitigating the misuse of AI-generated text. This survey introduces the pillars of AI-generated text forensics shown in Figure 1: (i) detection, (ii) attribution, and (iii) characterization — each serving its own purpose in combating the misuse of AI-generated content. Detection is key for distinguishing between human and AI-generated texts, a fundamental step in safeguarding information integrity. Attribution goes a step further by tracing AI-generated content back to its source model, promoting transparency and accountability. Characterization seeks to understand the intent behind AI-generated texts, which is crucial for preempting harmful content.

To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review of AI-generated text forensic systems, and it features a detailed taxonomy illustrated in Figure 2. This work is needed because of the evolving sophistication of AI-generated text and its potential misuse, which require a multi-faceted approach for analysis and mitigation. Therefore, this survey aims to organize current work and identify gaps and future directions in this rapidly developing field. Our work facilitates the advancement of research in AI-generated text forensics, contributing to more robust, transparent, and accountable digital information ecosystems. Related Surveys: Numerous surveys discuss aspects of detection [7,8,9] and attribution [10] in isolated contexts. In contrast, our survey aims to delineate the broad themes within the AI-generated forensics field by identifying its fundamental pillars, exploring their interconnections, and discussing challenges in a future where AI-generated text becomes pervasive.
